title: Firmament
content:
FIRMAMENT

The firmament is the Bible's word for the sky or the space above the earth. The original Hebrew word means something that is spread out or stretched over the earth. The ancient Hebrews likely understood the firmament as the open sky, where the clouds, the sun, and the moon are found.

On the second day of creation, God made the firmament above the earth. It separated the waters below from the waters above. God called the firmament “heaven” (Genesis 1:6–8). On the fourth day, God placed lights in the firmament. These lights marked day and night, seasons, days, and years. The greater light, the sun, ruled the day. The lesser light, the moon, ruled the night (verses 14–19). The firmament also contained the stars.

The Psalms use the word “firmament” twice. In both places, it refers to what God has made (Psalms 19:1; 150:1). In the books of Ezekiel (Ezekiel 1:22–26; 10:1) and Daniel (Daniel 12:3), the firmament is always related to God's creation.

title: First and Second Maccabees
content:
FIRST AND SECOND MACCABEES

First and Second Maccabees are two deuterocanonical books that cover the period of Israel’s history from 167 BC to 100 BC. These books are included in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, but not in Protestant or Jewish Bibles.

The books are named after Judas Maccabeus, who started the Jewish revolt against Rome in 166 BC. The importance of these books is that they provide historical accounts of Israel’s struggles during the time between Malachi (the last book of the Old Testament) and the time of Christ (6/5 BC–AD 30).

First Maccabees

Like 1 Chronicles and 2 Chronicles, this work was written to record a “spiritual” history of the nation. The difference is that 1 Maccabees exclusively describes the Maccabean period up to 100 BC. The unknown author used some genuine literary sources, although parts of the work may not be historical.

Second Maccabees

This book is written around 100 BC. It focuses more on theology than 1 Maccabees. 1 Maccabees seeks to present a reasonably objective account of the Hasmoneans while 2 Maccabees is a rhetorical summary of a considerably larger work on the subject of the Maccabean era.

See Maccabean Period.

title: First Book of Esdras
content:
FIRST BOOK OF ESDRAS

A book that is largely a compilation of material from 2 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah.

Preview

• Who Wrote the First Book of Esdras? When Was It Written?

• What Is the Background of the First Book of Esdras?

• What Happens in the First Book of Esdras?

Who Wrote the First Book of Esdras? When Was It Written?

The author of 1 Esdras is unknown. Bible scholars have different ideas of where it came from. There are three main possibilities:

  1. 1 Esdras might be the original Septuagint (ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament) version. Ezra and Nehemiah may contain changes made by Theodotion, who revised the Septuagint in the second century AD.

  2. 1 Esdras began as a Hebrew text not included in the Old Testament. That Hebrew text is now lost.

  3. 1 Esdras is an edited collection of pieces from the Septuagint translation of 2 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Most Bible scholars agree with this idea.

Esdras (also known as Ezra) was a descendant of Aaron’s priestly line. He was one of the leaders of the exiled Jews who returned to Judea from Babylon. His work as a leader and promoter of the law likely took place during the reign of Persian king Artaxerxes I from 465 to 424 BC.

1 Esdras must have been written before AD 90. This is likely because the first-century Jewish historian Josephus quoted from it. The most likely date of authorship is likely between 150 and 100 BC.

What Is the Background of the First Book of Esdras?

There are four books about Ezra and the restoration of the Jews in Judea after the exile. Two of those books, titled Ezra and Nehemiah, are accepted as Scripture by Jewish people, Roman Catholics, and Protestants alike. The other two, 1 Esdras and 2 Esdras, are not part of the Old Testament. However, they were included in the Latin Vulgate Bible (a translation by Jerome in AD 404). The Roman Catholic Council of Trent, which took place from 1545 to 1663, included 1 and 2 Esdras in the Old Testament scriptures as part of the apocryphal books. The books of Esdras in the Vulgate are named as follows:

  • 1 Esdras is named Ezra

  • 2 Esdras is named Nehemiah

  • 3 Esdras is named 1 Esdras

  • 4 Esdras is named 2 Esdras

What Happens in the First Book of Esdras?

First Esdras is a history of the Jews from the reign of King Josiah in Jerusalem, from 640 to 609 BC, through the ministry of Ezra. It describes the career of Ezra but does not mention Nehemiah. Originally written in Greek, 1 Esdras retells the material found in 2 Chronicles 35:1–36:23, Ezra 1:1–10:44, and Nehemiah 7:73–8:12. However, it removes Ezra 4:6 and moves 4:7–24 before 2:1. 1 Esdras adds two sections of material that are not in the Bible:

  • 1 Esdras 1:23–24 is a minor addition

  • 1 Esdras 3:1–4:63 is a major addition. It is a story about three youths who served Darius I of Persia, who ruled from 522 to 486 BC. They compete to decide if wine, power, or women are strongest. The third youth, Zerubbabel, argues that women are strongest but adds “truth” to his argument and wins. As a reward, he asks for permission to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem, and Darius agrees. The story ends with Zerubbabel planning to build the temple. 1 Esdras is different from Ezra and Nehemiah by placing Zerubbabel’s return to Judea under Darius I instead of Cyrus, who ruled from 559 to 530 BC.

FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK

title: First Jewish Revolt
content:
FIRST JEWISH REVOLT

The First Jewish Revolt was an uprising in AD 66–70, which occurred as the result of a series of ineffective Roman governors in Judea. After the last Jewish king, Agrippa I (the Herod of Acts 12), died in AD 44, the next 20 years were filled with persecution and humiliation for the Jews in Palestine.

For the unrest to become a revolt, only one more reason was needed. The final reason was provided by Florus, the Roman governor appointed in AD 64. He provoked the Jews into an uprising in the year 66 by demanding money from the temple treasury. Under his rule, Roman soldiers slaughtered and pillaged the Jews.

Rebellion quickly spread throughout Palestine, accompanied by a general struggle between Jews and pagans in several eastern Mediterranean cities. The revolt in Palestine was led by the Zealots, a Jewish group that had long wanted the Romans to leave Palestine. After an initial Jewish victory at the pass of Beth-horon, the emperor Nero dispatched his most able general, Vespasian, to direct the operation of punishing the rebels.

By the end of AD 67, all of Galilee and other northern lands were back under Roman rule. In AD 67 and 68 further operations in Samaria and Judea left only four strongholds in Jewish control. At this point, the Roman campaign slowed. Nero committed suicide in AD 68. After three short-lived emperors, General Vespasian gained control of the empire in AD 69. His son Titus took command of the forces in Palestine and laid siege to Jerusalem in AD 70.

The Jews in the capital might have been better prepared had they taken advantage of the turmoil in Rome to strengthen their own position and resolve disputes among warring Jewish groups. Instead, the arrival of Titus with 80,000 soldiers forced them to unify for a last defense of the city.

The siege of the city lasted for five months. Jerusalem fought heroically against the advancing Romans, forcing a slow conquest of the city. A tragic moment in Jewish history came early in August of AD 70 when for the first time in centuries the morning and evening sacrifices were not offered at the temple.

About 29 August, under circumstances still not clear, the sanctuary was burned and the temple destroyed. This fulfilled the prophecy of Jesus (Matthew 24:1–2; Mark 13:1–2; Luke 19:43–44; 21:5–7). For another month some resistance continued, but by the end of September, the conflict was over in the ruined city. In all, perhaps one million Jews were killed and 900,000 taken captive during the revolt.

See also History of Israel; Jerusalem; Judaism.

title: First Letter of John
content:
FIRST LETTER OF JOHN

First John is the first of three short letters attributed to John. It is a letter written to encourage believers and to warn them against false teaching.

Why Was First John Written?

First John is a simple but deep answer to false teaching that was threatening the church. The author responds by clearly explaining the truth found in Christ. He shows two different ways of thinking: the true way and the false way. He clearly shows the difference between them.

The letter also has a positive purpose. The author wants his "children" to know the truth. He wants them to respond to God, who has revealed himself in Christ: "We write these things so that our joy may be complete. And this is the message we have heard from Him and announce to you: God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all" (1 John 1:4–5).

The author further explains the positive goal in 5:20: "And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know Him who is true; and we are in Him who is true—in His Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life."

Understanding Christ as both God and man is very important to the author. Believers need to know this truth and remain in it. Then they can continue to abide in the Son of God. This means they can stay joined to him and trust him. They will not be led away by false teaching.

Who Were the False Teachers?

If the letter was written to answer the claims of false teachers, it helps us understand who they were. According to 1 John 2:19, these opponents had once been part of the Christian community. Later, they left the community to spread their own beliefs.

The false teachers made a serious error about Christ. They denied that Jesus was truly human. This also meant they denied that he was the Messiah, the one God promised to send. The false prophets can be known by what they confess about Jesus: “By this you will know the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God” (4:2). The opening verse of the letter also strongly answers this denial of the humanity of Jesus. First John 2:22 identifies the liar as the one “who denies that Jesus is the Christ … This is the antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son.”

These beliefs led to a serious problem in how people lived. The false teachers accepted a sinful way of life and did not care for others. So John calls these people back to right living and to love for other believers in Christ.

Scholars have identified John’s opponents in several ways. Their focus on secret knowledge may point to a Gnostic-type false teaching. Gnosticism claimed that special knowledge was needed to know spiritual truth. Their denial that Jesus was truly human may point to docetism. Docetism was a false teaching that said Jesus only seemed to be human.

Cerinthus of Asia Minor (mentioned by the early church father Irenaeus) has often been associated with the opposition in 1 John.

Who Wrote the First Letter of John?

A careful comparison of 1 John with the Gospel of John shows many similarities. The two books use similar words, style, and ideas. Both books often use words like:

  • "love,"

  • "life,"

  • "truth,"

  • "light,"

  • "Son,"

  • "Spirit,"

  • "advocate,"

  • "revealed,"

  • "sin,"

  • "world,"

  • "flesh,"

  • "abide,"

  • "know,"

  • "walk," and

  • "commandments."

They also use similar word groups. These include:

  • "Spirit of truth,"

  • "born of God,"

  • "children of God," and

  • "overcome the world."

These similarities may point to one author. The two books also use similar grammar and patterns of speech. They share many of the same theological ideas about God, Christ, and the Christian life.

It is difficult to deny the close connection between 1 John and the Gospel of John. Some scholars have tried to show differences between the two books. Even so, they often admit that the author of one book must have been closely connected to the author of the other. The author of one book also seems to have deeply influenced the author of the other.

The traditional view is that the apostle John wrote both the Gospel of John and 1 John. The opening words of 1 John clearly support this view: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands—this is the Word of life” (1:1). These words show that the author wanted readers to know he was an eyewitness. He had seen and touched Jesus.

Some scholars have questioned the traditional view because of a statement from Papias. Papias was bishop of Hierapolis in Asia Minor. He lived around AD 100–140. Eusebius, an early church historian, preserved Papias’s statement:

“If I met someone who followed the elders, I would ask about the elders' words—what Andrew, Peter, Thomas, James, John, Matthew, or any other of the Lord’s disciples said. I would also ask about what Aristion and the elder John, the Lord’s disciples, say.”

Some important scholars have argued that there was an elder John who was a different person from the apostle John. They believe this elder may have lived in Asia Minor. However, Irenaeus in Against Heresies and the Muratorian Fragment (both from the late second century AD) attribute 1 John to the apostle John.

The author’s claim to be an eyewitness and his tone of authority both point to the apostle John as the author of 1 John. Christian tradition says that John lived to an old age and taught in Ephesus. It also says that he continued to teach Christians to love one another until the end of his life. First John fits this kind of setting.

When Was the First Letter of John Written?

First John was probably written near the end of the first century. The false teaching that John rejects supports this date. So do later references to 1 John in the writings of Polycarp and Irenaeus. We cannot determine a more exact date with the current evidence.

What Variations Appear in the Manuscripts of the First Letter of John?

The text of 1 John has been preserved quite well. Its simple words and clear ideas helped people copy and preserve it accurately.

Three passages are important when discussing the text of 1 John.

  1. The word “all” in 1 John 2:20 appears in different forms in different manuscripts. Some manuscripts use the nominative case, which usually marks the subject of a sentence. Other manuscripts use the accusative case, which usually marks the object. The King James Version translates the verse as: “Ye know all things.” But the nominative case may give a better meaning: “All of you know.” In this reading, John is not saying that believers know everything. He is saying that all believers have received this knowledge.

  2. In 4:19, the earliest manuscripts do not include an object after the verb "love." Some later manuscripts add either “him” or “God” to the sentence. The Berean Standard Bible margin note mentions this difference. The King James Version follows the later manuscripts.

  3. The most famous textual variant in in 1 John is found in 5:7–8. The words "These three agree in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit..." were added to the text at a later date. They were not part of the earliest Greek manuscripts. The earliest known reference to these words comes from Priscillian, a Spanish teacher who was later judged to be a heretic. He died in AD 385. Later, these words were accepted into the Latin Vulgate.

    The scholar Erasmus, who edited the first published Greek Testament, did not include these words because they were missing in Greek manuscripts. The only Greek manuscripts that include these words were produced after Erasmus’s edition. For this reason, modern Bible translations usually do not include these words in 5:7–8.

What Is the First Letter of John About?

Scholars do not agree on the exact plan and structure of 1 John. The letter uses simple terms and a small group of repeated words. It also repeats many of the same ideas. Because of this, it is hard to make a clear outline of the letter. Some scholars describe the letter’s argument as “spiral.” This means that John returns to the same ideas again and again. He develops them more each time. The letter sounds like the teaching of an honored elder in the Christian community. He shares wisdom with his readers, but he does not present his ideas as a strict, step-by-step argument.

Chapter numbers were not added to the New Testament text until AD 1228. These divisions can sometimes interrupt the flow of thought. Still, they give us a helpful way to review the content of 1 John. First John also differs from the common letter style of the first century. Paul’s letters clearly show that common style.

The first chapter has two parts. It begins with an introduction. Then it explains what it means to walk in the light, or to live in God’s truth. This chapter clearly shows what God is like. It also shows how people can live in relationship with him.

Introduction

The introduction follows the strong and beautiful style of the opening words of the Gospel of John and the Letter to the Hebrews. It clearly states that the gospel message can be trusted. The author says that he was an eyewitness of Jesus, the one through whom the Father revealed himself. He says that he is simply proclaiming events that he himself experienced. The author stresses that he heard, saw, and touched Jesus. These words show that the coming of Jesus was not only a spiritual idea or a theory. Jesus truly came into the world and was known through human experience.

Chapter 1

The purpose of this message is fellowship. Fellowship means shared life and close relationship. The Greek word is koinonia. This fellowship works in two directions. First, believers share fellowship with one another. Second, believers share fellowship with the Father and the Son (1:3). The second purpose is "so that our joy may be complete" (verse 4).

In the main part of the letter, John quickly turns to the truth that “God is light” (1:5–10).

This truth has several important meanings:

  1. There is no darkness in God at all (verse 5). In this context, darkness does not mean physical darkness or night. Instead, it represents evil, falsehood, and everything opposed to God.

  2. People who walk in darkness cannot have fellowship with God. To walk in darkness means to live in sin and reject God’s truth (verse 6).

  3. People who walk in the light have fellowship with other believers. To walk in the light means to live in God’s truth. Jesus, God’s Son, also cleanses them from all sin (verse 7).

  4. All people have sinned. Denying this does not change the truth (verse 8).

  5. When people confess their sins, God forgives them and cleanses them. He does this because he is faithful and righteous (verse 9).

  6. People who deny that they have sinned are saying that God is not truthful. They also show that his word is not in them (verse 10).

Joy and fellowship are only for those who walk in the light of God’s presence. God is light, and he shows this light through his Son, Jesus Christ. The introduction of the Gospel of John reminds us that the Word brought light to all people. Through Jesus, God deals with the problem of sin and unrighteousness. He forgives people and cleanses them (that is, he removes their guilt and purifies them from sin).

Chapter 2

The second chapter continues the thought from the end of chapter 1. It explains how God solves the problem of sin. Then John speaks about the new commandment. He also warns readers about the threat of the antichrist.

In 2:1–6, John says more about how God solves the problem of sin. This matters because God is pure and without sin. Jesus Christ forgives sin and cleanses people from unrighteousness. This means he removes what is wrong and makes people right with God. Jesus is also our advocate before God. An advocate is someone who speaks for another person and helps that person. This is the same word (transliterated “Paraclete”) used in John 14–16, where it refers to the Holy Spirit. Jesus has made full reconciliation possible between God and humanity. Reconciliation means bringing people back into right relationship with God.

Believers should respond by obeying God’s commandments. The third verse is the first of several verses answering one question: How can believers know that these things are true? The first test is obedience. The implications of this test are positive in verses 3 and 5 and negative in verse 4. Verse 6 clearly shows that believers should model their way of life on Jesus.

Verses 7–17 describe the second test of believing, or “abiding in him.” To abide in Christ means to remain joined to him and trust him. The second test is love for other believers in the Christian community. John clearly says that a person cannot walk in God’s light and hate a Christian brother or sister at the same time. This develops the earlier idea of fellowship in the light.

After this, John encourages three groups of people (2:12–14). These groups may refer to different stages in the Christian life, not to different ages. Then John warns them not to love the world (2:15–17). In this context, the world means human desires and pride that are opposed to God. These desires and pride do not last. They do not come from the Father, who is light. Only the person who obeys God’s will will live forever.

John then addresses the problem of the last days and the coming of the antichrist (2:18–27). He also speaks about many antichrists. These people had once belonged to the Christian community (verse 19). Anyone who denies that Jesus is the Messiah belongs in this group. John also says that a person cannot deny Christ and still belong to God (verse 23). Those who are born of God have received an anointing from him (being set apart by God and helped by the Holy Spirit). This anointing helps them recognize the lies of the antichrist (verse 27).

Up to this point, the whole letter has focused on what it means to walk with God, who is light. God has revealed himself in Jesus. This gives believers clear understanding. It helps them know what is true and recognize what is false.

Chapter 3

The last two verses of chapter 2 introduce the new topic for chapter 3: being "born of Him" (2:29). The children of God do not fear God's final revelation at Christ's second coming. Instead, they anticipate it. Then their new birth will become fully visible (3:2). John pauses to celebrate how God's love works in our lives as his children (verse 1).

John turns from the joy of thinking about our place as God’s children to the hard truth about the world we live in. The world around us is marked by sin. John defines sin as “lawlessness” (3:4), which means living against God’s commands. Sin begins with the devil, “has been sinning from the very start” (verse 8). The “children of the devil” show who they are by living lawless lives (verses 10–12). John uses Cain as an example of this kind of life.

Jesus, whose second appearance is noted in the opening verses, came the first time to take away sins and destroy the works of the devil (3:5, 8). Those who follow Jesus should follow the pattern of their Father, who is righteous (verse 7). A righteous life is marked by purity and by turning away from sin (verses 3, 7–9). The difference between these two lifestyles is clear (verse 10).

The second half of chapter 3 focuses on showing that a person is in a right relationship with God through love for others in the Christian community. Verse 12 introduced the negative example with Cain. Hating a brother is like committing murder (3:15). Ignoring a brother or sister in need is also wrong (verses 17–18). Jesus, who gave his life for us, is the model for loving others (verse 16). Loving brothers and sisters shows that one is born of God and has moved from death to life (verse 14). The difference between God's spiritual children and the devil's children is evident.

The last half of chapter 3 emphasizes one of John's favorite themes. The phrase “We know” appears in verses 14, 16, 19, and 24. In a world of uncertainties, John recognizes the great need for assurance. So John gives several tests that help God’s children gain and keep this confidence.

Chapter 4

The transition to chapter 4 happens at the end of chapter 3: “we know that He remains in us: by the Spirit He has given us” (verse 24). Those with the Holy Spirit must tell the difference between the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error. The Spirit of truth comes from God. The spirit of error teaches what is false.

John then gives a test for true teaching. Those who have the Spirit of God confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. This means they confess that Jesus is God and that he became truly human (4:2–3). False prophets who deny this truth have "the spirit of the antichrist" (verse 3). Obeying God helps the children of God recognize and respond to God's message (verses 4–6).

In verses 7–12, John says that love comes from God, because God is love (verse 8). God clearly showed this love in Jesus. Through Jesus, God dealt with the problem of sin (verses 9–10). Because of this, God’s children should love one another (verse 11). When we love one another, God’s love reaches its goal in us (verse 12). In this paragraph, three ideas are closely connected: being born of God, loving God, and knowing God.

Verse 13 continues the message of assurance from 3:1: “By this we know that we remain in Him, and He in us: He has given us of His Spirit.” Believers also receive assurance when they confess that Jesus is the Son of God and the Savior of the world. This helps them know God’s love. God’s love then flows through believers to others. This love shows that they have a true relationship with God (4:14–21). This assurance is so strong that believers do not need to fear the day of judgment (verses 17–18).

Chapter 5

In the final chapter, John discusses the connection between love and a right relationship with God. Those born of God do not find God's commandments too difficult to obey (5:3). Their faith helps them overcome the world, which tries to keep them from obeying God (verse 4). This faith has its basis on Jesus as the Son of God (verse 5).

Once again, right belief is important. Jesus was fully human (verse 6), and the Spirit bears witness to the truth about Jesus (verses 7–8). The result is strong inner confidence that God "has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son" (verse 11). The difference between those who have life and those who do not is very clear. The person who has the Son has life. The person who does not have the Son does not have life (verse 12).

Verses 13–16 move from eternal life to confidence in prayer. Believers can pray with strong confidence in God. They can trust that God hears them and answers their prayers according to his will (verses 14–15). This confidence also applies to praying for others who sin. John describes sin as "unrighteousness" (lack of a right relationship with God), not the sin leading to death (verse 12). God will honor such prayers by giving life to the sinner (verse 16).

The final verses repeat the main themes of the letter. They emphasize the victory of those born of God through Jesus, the true God. This victory sets God's children apart from the world, which is under the power of the evil one. The letter ends with a strong note of assurance.

See also Letters of John; John, the Apostle.

title: First Letter to the Corinthians
content:
FIRST LETTER TO THE CORINTHIANS

The First Letter to the Corinthians is one of the letters the apostle Paul wrote to the church in Corinth. In this letter, Paul answered questions from the believers and addressed problems that had developed in the church. He encouraged them to live in unity, grow in holiness, and use their spiritual gifts to serve one another. The letter also contains important teaching about Christ’s death and resurrection, the Lord’s Supper, love, and the future resurrection of believers.

Preview

  • Who Wrote the First Letter to the Corinthians?

  • When and Where Was the First Letter to the Corinthians Written?

  • What Was the Background of the First Letter to the Corinthians?

  • Why Was the First Letter to the Corinthians Written? What Does It Teach Us?

  • What Is the Content of the First Letter to the Corinthians?

Who Wrote the First Letter to the Corinthians?

Scholars agree that the apostle Paul wrote 1 Corinthians. He wrote it during his third missionary journey while living in Ephesus. By then, Paul was a mature missionary, about 55 years old. He had significant experience from starting churches in about a quarter of the Mediterranean world.

When and Where Was the First Letter to the Corinthians Written?

Paul worked in Corinth from around AD 50 to 52. After a short stay in Jerusalem, he returned to his missionary work in Ephesus (Acts 19), where he served for three years (AD 53–55/56). During this time, he wrote at least three letters to Corinth. He also visited Corinth during this time.

His first letter, often called "the previous letter," is mentioned in 1 Corinthians 5:9–11. This reference shows that people misunderstood the letter. However, we know little about what it said because the letter has been lost.

In AD 55, Paul heard reports from Chloe’s household (1 Corinthians 1:11). They were probably members of the church that met in her home. Paul then dictated a second letter to the church in Corinth. This letter is now known as 1 Corinthians. Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus probably delivered the letter to Corinth (16:17).

Paul later wrote a third letter to Corinth, called "the letter of tears" (2 Corinthians 2:2–3). After that, he wrote the letter we now call 2 Corinthians.

What Was the Background of the First Letter to the Corinthians?

Corinth was a seaport city. The Romans destroyed it in 146 BC and Julius Caesar rebuilt it in 46 BC. After 27 BC, it became the Roman capital of Achaia. The Roman governor, called a proconsul, lived there (Acts 18:12).

The city itself was actually three cities:

  • the port of Cenchrea, about 13 kilometers (eight miles) to the east, where ships from the Aegean Sea unloaded;

  • the port of Lechaion, about 1.6 kilometers (a mile) to the west on the Gulf of Corinth, where ships reloaded after transporting goods over the isthmus using wagons and rollers; and

  • the city of Corinth itself, located on the high ground in between the two ports.

The acropolis of the city, on top of the steep and high Acrocorinth, had the temple of Aphrodite. Here, 1,000 female slaves served this goddess of love. This unique Corinthian cult worshipped Aphrodite, the goddess of love, beauty, and fertility, who is similar to the Roman Venus. These religious practices led to widespread moral decline. Corinthian morals were famously corrupt, even compared to pagan Rome.

In the city below was the synagogue (Acts 18:4). Although the city, as a Roman colony, was mostly Italian, it attracted other Mediterranean peoples, including Jews.

Why Was the First Letter to the Corinthians Written? What Does It Teach Us?

Paul's main concern in 1 Corinthians was the unity of the church. In Corinth, people were self-centered, forming cliques within the church. They showed off their knowledge and freedom, upsetting others. They also acted selfishly during worship services.

The book highlights two major concerns.

  1. Corinth's relaxed sexual ethics, along with other pagan practices, had influenced the church. Paul needed to set boundaries.

  2. There was a problem accepting the resurrection of the body. Paul understood this issue affected the core of the faith and strongly affirmed the resurrection.

Some scholars have connected these last two issues, along with parts of the conflict over unity, especially the Corinthians’ concern with knowledge, to ideas found in Gnosticism. They therefore conclude that Paul was opposing a Gnostic group in Corinth.

However, a careful study suggests a different conclusion. Some ideas present in Corinth later helped shape Gnosticism, a religious movement that emphasized special spiritual knowledge. But it would be historically inaccurate to call these first-century ideas fully Gnostic. We may recognize early forms of ideas that later appeared in Gnosticism, but we should interpret the situation in its first-century setting.

Paul focused on the church's unity and purity. He worked to prevent the church from splitting into groups arguing over moral and doctrinal issues. He also wanted the church to stay focused on Jesus, the exalted Lord.

What Is the Content of the First Letter to the Corinthians?

Greeting, 1:1–9

Paul starts with a typical greeting and then offers his usual prayer of thanks. Two things are notable. First, the greeting mentions Sosthenes alongside Paul. We are not certain who Sosthenes was, but the Corinthians likely knew him well. He was probably the Sosthenes identified in Acts 18:17 as the synagogue leader after Crispus converted.

Second, Paul emphasizes the Corinthians' skills in speech, knowledge, and spiritual gifts. They possessed all of these, and they were genuine. However, they were misusing these good things. Paul's solution is not to suppress these gifts (he thanks God for them), but to use them in a new way.

Report from Chloe’s People, 1:10–4:21

The Corinthians had turned Paul, Cephas (the Greek Peter used), Apollos, and even Christ into leaders of different groups. We do not know exactly what each group believed. However, it is possible that the Pauline group focused on Paul's ideas of freedom. The Petrine group might have emphasized following Jewish traditions. The Apollos group likely valued philosophical understanding and speaking skills.

Regardless of their beliefs, Paul was upset that these divisions harmed their unity. He first explained that his actions were not meant to gain followers but to guide people to Christ. He did not insist on baptizing converts himself because it did not matter who performed the baptisms. They were all baptized into Christ.

Paul quickly addresses the main issue: some people want to appear better or wiser than others who lack their group's insights in the church. Their pursuit of wisdom goes against Paul's message of the gospel.

First, the message of a crucified Christ (1:18) did not fit the wisdom and values of Jews or Greeks. It required a completely new perspective on life—God's perspective.

Second, God did not choose them based on their social status. Instead, he gave them equal status through him (1:26–31).

Third, their faith was not based on Paul's speaking skills but on the gifts of the Spirit that Paul showed (2:4). These demonstrations of gift convinced them that God was working through Paul. It was God's Spirit, not arguments, that led them to God. Therefore, the Spirit, not human reasoning, would continue to reveal God to them. They needed to reject worldly reasoning and shift to an understanding of life from the Spirit's perspective, which provides true wisdom.

Fourth, they were not acting spiritually when they claimed Paul and others as party leaders. This shows the human tendency to focus on people instead of God, who works equally in everyone.

Fifth, these servants worked together to build one "temple" for God, based on the foundation of Jesus Christ, which is the church. God alone will judge how each Christian helps build the church. But beware of anyone who divides the church, for "if anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him" (3:17). (Note that here the temple imagery refers to the church as a whole. In chapter 6, it will refer to each Christian individually as the temple.)

Finally, he highlights their exaggerated view of the end times. With their genuine spiritual gifts and worldly wisdom, they claimed to reign with Christ (4:8–13). Paul, using ironic sarcasm, shows how different this claim is from the apostles' lifestyle. The apostles lived like Jesus, enduring suffering and expecting exaltation later. The Corinthians wanted exaltation now without experiencing hardship.

Paul ends this section with a warning. He gently encourages those who might listen to follow his example. He believes his life is the message (verses 14–16). Timothy will also live out the truth in front of them. Then, he warns the "arrogant" (verse 18), stating he will test their spiritual power, not just their words, if he visits.

The Report from the Corinthian Messengers, 5:1–6:20

Paul now addresses three issues reported by messengers who brought him the Corinthians' letter.

The first issue is church discipline (5:12–13). Paul mentions a case of obvious immorality—incest. This behavior was so clearly wrong that even non-Christians found it immoral. It was not due to ignorance of Christian values. Furthermore, the church had not acted but instead boasted about its tolerance. This might have been due to a misunderstanding of Paul’s teaching on freedom from the law.

Paul presents three principles in this section:

  1. the main goal of church discipline is to help the offender repent and return;

  2. the secondary goal is to protect the church (5:6–8); and

  3. the church should not judge or control the actions of evil people in the world. Those roles of judgement and power belong to God. The church should discipline those within the church (verses 9–13).

Paul will also use these principles in the following chapters (compare 7:12–16).

The second issue is lawsuits between Christians (6:1–11). Corinthian society was as prone to lawsuits as ours, and Christians did not see anything wrong with suing each other. Paul was troubled. If Christians are to judge the world, they should not involve outsiders in church matters. Paul says Christians should work together to resolve cases within the church and avoid taking cases to "those of no standing in the church" (6:4, meaning non-Christian judges).

Paul suggests a better way than using pagan courts: simply accept the wrong (1 Corinthians 6:7). He applies the teachings of Jesus literally (Matthew 5:38–42) and argues that it is better to allow themselves to be cheated.

However, the Corinthians are willing to harm their fellow Christians to claim what they believe are their rights. This raises the question of whether greed still exists in their hearts (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). Paul accepts people who did evil in the past (because Jesus has cleansed them). But even if people claim to be believers, Paul clarifies that anyone who continues to practice greed or immorality is not part of the kingdom.

The final issue in this section is casual sexual intercourse (6:12–20). This was a world where virginity was important for women who wanted to marry. In Corinth temple slaves of Aphrodite served as prostitutes, and prostitution was the main form of casual sex. The libertine group used two slogans:

  • "Everything is permissible for me," possibly from Paul’s teaching, and

  • "Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food."

The second saying means that if the body works this way, it must be the Creator’s purpose. Paul clarifies rather than opposes their slogans. Freedom is secondary to other goals (6:12, 20). The body is not for personal use, but should be dedicated to the Lord, as the doctrine of the resurrection shows (verses 13–14).

Furthermore, sexual intercourse involves the whole person, unlike eating (Paul refers to Genesis 2:24; see also Jesus in Matthew 19:5). This act takes a person from the body of Christ and unites them with a prostitute (1 Corinthians 6:15–17). Immorality is different from other sins, which are external to the self, because it changes the self and defiles the body, where the Holy Spirit lives. It ignores that Christ has redeemed the body and that the entire Christian belongs to God, not to themselves.

Paul's Responses to the Corinthians, 7:1–16:4

Now Paul addresses the issues raised by the Corinthians. He expands somewhat on the answers he has already provided to their unasked questions.

The first issue is marriage (7:1–24). The ascetic group in Corinth, possibly reacting against the libertines of chapter 6, used the slogan "It is good to abstain from sexual relations" (7:1). The Corinthians had begun suggesting that married Christians, not just the unmarried, should avoid sexual relations. Paul clarified this with three points.

  • First, he said total abstinence is unrealistic because it could lead to immorality (verses 2, 7–9).

  • Second, when people get married they no longer own their own bodies; their bodies belong to each other for their mutual benefit (verses 3–4). Refusing sexual relations without mutual agreement denies the other spouse what Paul says is due within marriage.

  • Third, abstinence is allowed for short periods by mutual agreement as a type of fast to focus on Christ (verse 5).

Paul will discuss the topic of being unmarried more in 7:25–40. He mentions that he is happy being unmarried. However, since not everyone has this ability, it is better to express sexuality fully in marriage than to struggle with desire (7:7–9). Once two Christians marry, divorce is not an option. Christ's clear teachings confirm this (Matthew 5:31–32; Mark 10:11–12; Luke 16:18 and similar passages). There are no exceptions.

Paul perhaps does not know about the exception mentioned in Matthew 19:9. He may have interpreted that exception as referring to premarital unfaithfulness discovered before marriage, not to adultery after marriage. Although sometimes a Christian couple may need to live apart, they should always aim for reconciliation. The teachings of Jesus do not allow thinking of marriage as ending (1 Corinthians 7:10–11).

What if the spouse is not a Christian? Paul addresses a situation where Jesus did not give specific guidance.

  • First, Jesus told Christians not to divorce, so even here, the Christian should not initiate divorce proceedings (7:12–13).

  • Second, Christians should not control or judge non-Christians (6:12–13). If the non-Christian partner wants a divorce, the Christian does not have to stay in the relationship (7:15).

  • Third, staying in an unequal partnership is no shame to a Christian. Paul says even an unequal relationship can become holy, benefiting the children and possibly leading to the spouse's salvation (7:14, 16). This does not mean staying in abusive situations, but it encourages faithfulness in a mixed marriage.

Paul believes people usually do not need to change their life situation to serve Christ (7:17–24). Each person should generally stay in the life situation they were in when called to Christ. Paul uses examples like marriage or singleness, Jew (circumcision) or Gentile, and slave or free. He does not refer to situations that might be immoral. For slaves, they can accept freedom if it is available, but it does not change their true state before God or their ability to serve Christ (verses 21–23).

The second issue is about unmarried people (7:25–40). Paul says single people and widows can marry—it is not wrong. However, he suggests they stay single. Since everything in this age is temporary, staying single can help avoid the extra challenges marriage brings (25–31). Marriage divides attention between God and the spouse's needs. One should not neglect their spouse to serve God, but staying single allows full focus on God (32–35). If marriage is expected, the person should decide whether to marry for the woman's sake (and possibly the family's) or to care for her as a single person (36–38). Paul ends by repeating his main ideas (39–40).

The third issue Paul addresses is food offered to idols (8:1–11:1). Most meat in the marketplace came from animals sacrificed in temples as a dedicatory sacrifice. Scrupulous Jews would avoid all this meat. Additionally, pagans invited Christians to dinners in their homes and private feasts in pagan temples. Trade guilds also held feasts in pagan temples. Paul discusses these issues to teach broader principles of Christian behavior.

First, love, not knowledge, guides correct behavior (8:1–13). Some Corinthians felt superior because they believed idols were not real, and thus any food offered to them was still okay to eat. Paul acknowledges their beliefs but counters with, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (verse 1).

God cares less about what we know or eat and more about whether we love our fellow Christians. The concern is not that a fellow Christian might become angry if someone indulges, but that they might have a weak conscience and indulge themselves. If they eat the meat, even though they believe it is wrong, this leads them into rebelling against Christ. Leading someone astray is not love. It is better to avoid eating meat than to lead a fellow Christian into sin.

Second, he emphasizes that one should put others' interests, especially those of Christ and his gospel, before their own (9:1–23). The apostles expected the church to support them and their families (see Luke 10:5–7). Scripture shows that Paul had the right to ask for support from the Corinthians.

However, he usually made tents to support his ministry, although he accepted gifts from other churches. Paul did this to prevent people from thinking he was selling religion for profit (9:12) and for the personal satisfaction of doing more than required (verses 16–17). This was part of Paul's broader approach of putting his own preferences and interests below those of Christ and his gospel (verses 19–23).

Third, the confidence of the strong who show their freedom without considering other Christians is spiritually risky (9:24–10:22). What matters is not who starts but who finishes the Christian journey. Therefore, it requires discipline, not relaxed freedom (9:24–27).

Israel in the wilderness serves as an example of failure. They experienced "baptism" and "the Lord’s Supper" (10:2–4), like the church, but most did not reach the Promised Land. God destroyed them because they turned to sin. Similarly, Christians must be careful not to become so proud of their faith and freedom that they ignore sin and fall away (12). However, Christians should not be afraid, as temptation is not stronger than they are. God has provided a way out if they choose to take it (13).

Another link between the Israelites and the Corinthians involves participating in a sacrificial meal (10:14–22). In the Lord’s Supper, people share in the blood and body of Christ, similar to Israel’s sacrifices on the altar. Food offered to idols is also a sharing, not with the supposed god, but with the real demon behind the idol. Trying to share at both tables provokes God’s jealousy, just as Israel did (verse 22).

The summary connects the three chapters (10:23–11:1). Since offering food to idols does not change it, and all food belongs to God, you may eat anything sold in the market without asking questions (10:25–26). Similarly, a Christian may eat anything served at a dinner in an unbeliever's home.

However, if someone mentions the food was offered to idols, the Christian should avoid it. This is not because it harms him, but out of respect for the person who raised the concern. The Christian cares about his neighbor's well-being (verses 27–30).

In other words, follow Paul's example as he follows Christ, who served others rather than himself. Act so that God's reputation and character are evident, even in what you eat (verse 31). Try not to offend anyone but aim to help each person move toward salvation (verse 32).

The fourth issue Paul addresses is order in church meetings (11:2–14:40). The Corinthians' house churches had lively meetings. However, instead of showing unity in Christ, they showed selfishness. Paul did not want to change their activities; he wanted to change their approach.

The first problem in the meetings was the behavior of married women (11:1–16). At that time, wearing a veil or having a distinctive hairstyle showed a woman was married, similar to wearing a ring today. Paul had no problem with women praying and delivering prophecies in church. However, the women might have thought this freed them from their husbands (see Mark 12:25) and used it as a reason to remove their veils.

Paul argues that husband and wife are closely connected, just as humans are to God (1 Corinthians 11:3). Therefore, just as humans should honor God, a wife should respect her husband. While Paul supports women in ministry, he prioritizes marriage.

The second issue in the meetings was about class distinctions (11:17–34). Until the weekly Lord’s Supper became the sacrifice of the Mass in the third and fourth centuries, it was a shared meal. Middle- and upper-class Christians had more free time to arrive earlier at church gatherings. They had more money to bring better food and drink for themselves.

Following the customs of pagan clubs, they felt no guilt about starting early and feasting according to their class, as long as they also provided simple food for the slaves and peasants who could not arrive early (verse 21). This embarrassed the poorer Christians and made them feel the class differences strongly (verse 22). Paul argues that this is not the Lord’s Supper but a false version (verse 20).

Paul repeats the words of institution to show that they are all sharing in Christ’s body and blood (see 10:16–17), not their own meal. Maintaining divisions and class distinctions in the body of the church disrespects this meal. It's a participation that is unworthy because it undermines the unity of his body, the church (see 11:29), and invites his judgment, which they were already facing. Instead, they should examine their motives and truly gather as one to eat this shared meal.

The third issue in their meetings was the use of spiritual gifts (12:1–14:40). Some people in these house churches were influenced by early forms of Gnosticism that view the spiritual as good and the material as evil. When they felt inspired by a spirit they shouted, "Jesus [referring to the human Jesus, not the spiritual Christ] be cursed." Paul argues that it is not the Spirit of God saying this, because the Spirit in us declares the basic Christian confession, "Jesus is Lord."

Some people in these churches were overly proud of their own gifts, especially speaking in tongues. They would interrupt others or not let them speak. Paul argues that there is only one Spirit who gives all the gifts (12:4–6). The Spirit shows himself in each Christian, not just for their own benefit, but for everyone's good (verse 7). Since Christians have the Spirit, not just one gift, the gifts shown can change from meeting to meeting.

The same Spirit unites all Christians as one in Christ (12:12–13). The Spirit gives all the gifts, and all are equally inspired. Every gift is necessary for the body of Christ to function properly (verses 14–26). No one should feel less a part of the body if they lack a certain gift. In fact, the less noticeable gifts might be more important. Within the body of Christ, there are different ways the Spirit shows through individuals in a meeting. There are also different roles or functions for individuals in the body (verses 27–31).

It is not the display of a specific gift that shows one's spirituality, but how one uses it—with love (13:1–13). A gift used selfishly may be genuine, but it is worthless to the person (verses 1–3). Love is the opposite of selfishness (verses 4–7). The gifts of the Spirit are only needed between the first and second comings of Jesus. When God's kingdom is fully revealed and Jesus is present, these gifts will no longer be necessary (verses 10, 12). It is not giftedness but faith and hope that will be rewarded. Love is the greatest of these because it will continue as Christians live in perfect love with each other and with Jesus (verse 13).

In Corinth, Paul argues that while everyone should desire all gifts, the priority of love suggests greater reliance on the gift of prophecy for church meetings (14:1–25) The Corinthians had been focusing on speaking in tongues. Tongues without interpretation benefit only the speaker. It does not help others and can be confusing to outsiders or new believers. Outside church meetings, tongues have a role as a sign of judgment (21) and for private devotion (18), but inside, they need interpretation. Prophecy, however, builds up, exhorts, and convicts, so it should be sought in meetings.

In church meetings, both gifts and order should prevail (14:26–40). All types of gifts can be expressed to help everyone, not for selfish display (verse 26). Those who speak in tongues need an interpreter. Both they and prophets should speak one at a time, with time taken to evaluate the messages after every few speakers (verses 27–33). Women may have been talking during the service possibly due to habits developed in Jewish synagogues, where women sat separately and did not participate. Paul exhorts them to stop talking, pay attention, and learn. They should ask questions at home if they do not understand (verses 34–36). In his summary, Paul states that everything should be done in an orderly way (verses 37–40).

The fifth issue Paul addresses is the resurrection of the dead (chapter 15). Earlier problems, such as loose morals (chapters 5–6), ascetic denial, and sexuality (chapter 7), or believing one was already resurrected (chapter 15), suggest that some Corinthians did not believe in the resurrection of the body. However, they seemed to believe in the resurrection of Jesus and the immortality of the human soul.

Paul emphasizes that the resurrection of Jesus is an essential part of the gospel message (15:1–19). The church consistently taught that Jesus died, rose again, and appeared to many witnesses (verses 3–11). If they argued against the resurrection, then Christ could not have risen. If this were true, the entire gospel message would be false, and their hopes for salvation would be pointless (verses 12–19).

Since Christ has been raised, Christians will also be raised because they are united with him (15:20–28). Just as they experienced the effects of being in Adam, they will now experience the effects of being in Christ. However, resurrection does not happen all at once. It occurs in stages:

  • Christ was raised first;

  • Christians will be raised when he returns;

  • Christ must reign until he establishes his kingdom over the entire world, defeating all evil forces, including death; and then

  • Christ will hand over the perfected kingdom to the Father (verses 23–28).

The hope of resurrection explains Christian practices like baptizing people on behalf of those who had died. This likely refers to people who turned to Christ but died before baptism (15:29). It also explains the willingness to risk death for Christ (30–32).

Paul acknowledges intellectual challenges here. These challenges are resolved by understanding that resurrection involves both continuity and change (15:35–50). Just as a seed and plant are the same yet different, and as many types of bodies exist, so it is with the resurrection. What was perishable, dishonorable, weak, and physical (in Adam) will be raised as imperishable, glorious, powerful, and spiritual (in Christ). Christians must become like Christ, the heavenly man, to join God's kingdom.

Paul excitedly shares his hope for transformation (15:51–58). When Christ returns, the dead will rise and transform. The living will also transform instantly, becoming immune to death. Then, they will fully understand the victory already present in the resurrection of Jesus (verses 54–57). A final summary concludes that this teaching should assure them of a reward for anything done for Christ now (verse 58).

The sixth issue Paul addresses is the collection for the needy church in Jerusalem (16:1–4). A famine in Judea during the 40s left the church there poor. To meet this need and promote church unity, Paul organized a collection in some of his churches for the Judean church.

He answers the Corinthians' questions by saying the collection should be weekly and based on ability, not all at once when he arrives (16:2). When he comes, he will send the money with their chosen messengers. Paul is unclear about whether he will join them, easing concerns that he might benefit personally (compare 2 Corinthians 8–9).

Final Remarks and Closing, 16:5–24

Paul shares his travel plans, including a long visit after leaving Ephesus (compare 2 Corinthians 1). Timothy might arrive with the letter or soon after another mission. They should respect him and help him return. Paul explains he encouraged Apollos to visit Corinth to show he supports him.

He ends with advice to stay strong in faith and love, followed by his usual greetings. He praises the Corinthian messengers who brought him their letter (16:15–18). He sends greetings from Aquila and Prisca (Priscilla), who helped him start the church in Corinth (Acts 18:2–3, 18). He mentions the church's tradition of greeting each other with a kiss on each cheek (16:20).

Paul then takes the pen from the scribe, as was usual, and writes the closing message. He warns those who do not love Jesus, uses the Aramaic phrase “Come, O Lord” (Marana tha, possibly used to end services), and assures them of his love (verses 21–24).

See also Book of the Acts of the Apostles; Corinth; Second Letter to the Corinthians; Paul the Apostle.
